transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-07-10 15:00 PDT | Duration: 42m | Attendees: Alicia Park (Redwood AE), Samir Gupta (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (CTO, BlueHalo), Liam Ortiz (Lead ML Engineer, BlueHalo), Nadia Kline (Head of Product, BlueHalo)

[00:00] Alicia: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alicia from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account and I'll do a quick intro, Samir who's our systems engineer will run the demo.
[00:06] Maya: Hi thanks, excited — we've been looking at structured output patterns and function calling cause we need strict JSON for downstream ETL.
[00:12] Samir: Great, quick agenda: 1) show API/Console flow for JSON mode and schema enforcement, 2) function/tool calling example (webhook and internal service call), 3) discuss guardrails, retries, and performance tradeoffs, 4) Q&A and next steps.
[00:28] Nadia: Sounds good. Our primary concern is reliability of the JSON and avoiding hallucinated fields — we have strict data contracts to our analytics pipeline.
[00:36] Samir: Totally, that's where Redwood's structured output and functions features come in. We'll show the JSON schema enforcement in the Console then show a function call that maps to your downstream ingestion endpoint.
[00:45] Liam: Quick question before you start, what's the usual latency hit when you enforce strict JSON vs free text? Our SLAs are tight for user-facing flows.
[00:54] Samir: Good call. In our experience JSON-mode adds minimal overhead — typically 10-25ms on top of base generation for small payloads, bigger factor is model choice and sequence length; we'll show a 2k token example later. But the key is fewer post-processing retries so overall pipeline latency often improves.
[01:14] Maya: And on the model side, do you force a single model or do you do routing for cheaper models for background jobs?
[01:21] Alicia: You can pin models per route; we also support smart routing and fallback. For production we often recommend a primary low-latency open model and a higher-quality fallback for edge cases.
[01:31] Samir: Alright demo — I'm sharing my screen, Console -> Models -> Structured Output demo workspace. First I'm creating a JSON schema: top-level object with fields: patient_id (string), diagnosis_codes (array of strings), confidence (number 0-1), notes (string).
[01:50] Samir: I toggle "Enforce schema" which activates validation on the response and auto-retry strategies. If the model returns invalid JSON we can auto-repair by asking the model to reformat or run a deterministic parser fallback.
[02:08] Liam: How deterministic is the repair step? We can't get arbitrary fields introduced by the repair.
[02:13] Samir: The repair can be configured. We have strict mode which rejects invalid responses and returns a structured error to your application, and permissive mode which attempts fixes. You choose based on your SLOs.
[02:24] Maya: What about function calling vs webhooks? We want the model to call an internal API to create an event in our system.
[02:30] Samir: Two patterns: 1) Function calling — the model emits a structured function call (name + args) that Redwood can either execute via a secure connector or return to you to execute. 2) Tooling/webhook — Redwood can proxy calls into your VPC endpoint with mTLS if you want us to run the call.
[02:48] Nadia: Proxying into our VPC is interesting but we need KMS/HSM key integration for payload encryption.
[02:54] Alicia: We support KMS integrations and can integrate with customer-managed keys in our Private offering; for hosted we support envelope encryption with customer keys in some regions, and Dedicated gives more options. We'll follow up with the security pack.
[03:07] [03:07] Samir: Now I'm switching to the API tab — here's a simple curl example in JSON mode. Note the schema parameter; when you post messages you can set \"response_format\": {\"type\":\"json_schema\",\"schema\": \"<your-schema-here>\"}. The runtime validates and returns either the structured JSON or a detailed error object.
[03:28] Liam: Could you paste that example to the chat?
[03:31] Samir: Yep pasted — link: https://redwood.example/docs/structured-output (note: demo link)
[03:36] [03:36] Maya: There's often worry about models inventing IDs. Do you support deterministic ID generation or we should generate IDs client-side?
[03:43] Samir: We recommend you generate canonical IDs client-side for write operations; for inferred fields we expose provenance flags and confidence scores plus explain tokens. In the schema we included a \"confidence\" float so downstream can reject low-confidence items.
[03:57] [04:00] Alicia: Can we show function-calling example? Samir, over to you.
[04:02] Samir: Sure. I'm switching to a chat example where the model is asked to extract a structured diagnosis and then call a function create_patient_event(patient_id, payload). The model returns a function call json string that looks like: {\"name\":\"create_patient_event\",\"arguments\":{\"patient_id\":\"1234\",\"payload\":{...}}} but note transcription: on screen it renders as clean JSON.
[04:30] Samir: We then have Redwood configured to execute that call by hitting a webhook in your VPC. For demo purposes it's hitting a simulated endpoint.
[04:40] Liam: If the function fails (500), what's Redwood do? Retries? Dead-letter?
[04:45] Samir: You can configure retry policies and fallbacks. For idempotent operations we retry with backoff; for non-idempotent we bubble an error back to the client or send to a dead-letter queue, depending on your config.
[04:57] Maya: What about observability — we need token-level tracing and per-route success/failure metrics.
[05:03] Samir: Console has per-route metrics, token cost breakdowns, and tracing hooks that you can forward to Datadog or our analytics. We also attach model provenance and function_call logs to each request context.
[05:20] [05:20] Nadia: Are there limits on function arg size? We will sometimes have 3-4KB payloads in the payload.
[05:26] Samir: Function args are limited by request size (model context). For large payloads we recommend storing the blob in S3 and passing a reference key; Redwood supports signed temp URLs or VPC file proxies.
[05:36] Liam: Let's talk about cost — do schema enforcement and function calling increase token counts? It seems like additional system messages and validation will add tokens.
[05:45] Alicia: Yes there's overhead: system prompts and potential re-asks add tokens. But we offset that by needing fewer downstream repairs and by using batching and caching. Optimize will surface cost/perf tradeoffs and recommend quantized model variants for non-critical paths.
[06:00] [06:00] Maya: Security review concerns: SOC 2, SAML SSO, audit logs, data residency — we'll need your security questionnaire and SOC reports.
[06:08] Alicia: We'll send the SOC 2 + ISO docs and an SSO integration guide. For Private deployments we can meet stricter residency/KMS/HSM needs.
[06:16] Samir: Back to the demo — now I'm showing a schema mismatch: model returned \"diagnosis_codes\": \"E11.9\" instead of an array. Console highlights the error, we can click \"auto-repair\" which runs a constrained re-generation with a strict schema-enforcing system prompt. Note: in strict mode it returns a 400-style structured error to your app.
[06:45] Liam: I see that but worried about silent fixes that change meaning. Is there a change log?
[06:50] Samir: Yes all auto-repairs are logged with a diff and the provenance field that indicates what was modified. You can configure auto-repair to require manual approval for a rollout.
[07:02] [07:02] Maya: For the PoC, we need a bench with our real prompts and 95th percentile latency under 400ms for user flows, and correctness at 99% for required JSON fields. Can you commit to a benchmark run?
[07:15] Samir: We can run the bench; we'd need your sample prompts and an endpoint to test against or a representative traffic dump. We'll run both single-request latency and throughput tests and share cost estimates.
[07:26] Alicia: We'll scope that in the pilot proposal.
[07:29] [07:29] Nadia: Any discussion about private deployment options — we have PHI concerns and might need on-prem in the long term.
[07:35] Alicia: For PHI we typically recommend Private (VPC or on-prem), with customer-managed KMS, audit logs, and SOC 2+HIPAA addenda. We'll pull the security team into the next call to discuss specifics.
[07:47] Liam: Regarding SDKs — we prefer Python and Go. Do you have examples for function calling and structured outputs?
[07:52] Samir: Yes, SDKs support the structured schema param and function-calling wrappers. I'll share snippets after the call.
[07:58] [08:00] Maya: A couple of nitty-gritty: can we set per-route model pinning and force a fallback to non-hosted Dedicated pool if latency spikes?
[08:08] Samir: Yes, routing policies can prefer Dedicated or regional pools and have fallback rules to hosted variants. Autoscaling and reserved capacity help with burst protection.
[08:18] Alicia: Anything else from BlueHalo?
[08:21] Maya: One more — do you support role-based access for Console editing of schemas and function endpoints? We don't want product to change schemas without infra sign-off.
[08:28] Samir: Console RBAC supports per-team roles; editing certain resources can be scoped to admin roles only. We also have audit logs.
[08:36] [08:36] Nadia: Ok let's talk timeline — our procurement window is late July, engineering PoC in August. Is that realistic?
[08:44] Alicia: Yes, if we get the pilot signed mid-July we can kick off and have a 4-week PoC in August. We'll send the pilot doc today.
[08:53] [09:00] Samir: Quick demo wrap-up: showed schema enforcement, auto-repair vs strict reject, function calling execution into VPC, retry policies, observability, and Optimize suggestions.
[09:11] Maya: Thanks, that was helpful.
[09:14] Alicia: Recap/next steps: 1) Alicia to send pilot pricing + contract 2) Samir to run bench with Liam's sample prompts 3) Liam to share prompts and desired schemas 4) schedule security deep-dive to review SOC 2/HIPAA specifics.
[09:28] Maya: We'll expect the docs and proposal by Monday, thanks.
[09:31] Alicia: Great, thanks everyone. End.
